204	New read models, added to the wire crate:
205	
206	- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
207	- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
208	- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
209	- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
210	  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
211	  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
212	  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
213	  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
214	  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
215	  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
216	  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
217	- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.

221	### 4.4 WebSocket events
222	
223	Envelope:
224	
225	```json
226	{
227	  "server_id": "uuid",
228	  "epoch": "uuid",
229	  "revision": 1042,
230	  "type": "changed",
231	  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
232	  "at_ms": 1760220000000
233	}
234	```
235	
236	Event types:
237	
238	- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
239	- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
240	- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
241	- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
242	- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
243	- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.
244	
245	**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:
246	
247	1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
248	2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
249	   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
250	   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
251	   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
252	   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
253	   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
254	3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.
255	
256	**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.
257	
258	**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.
259	
260	**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:
261	
262	1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
263	2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
264	3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
265	4. enables commands.
266	
267	Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.

269	### 4.5 Commands
270	
271	- `send`, `resume` and `trust` are authenticated actions under `control` scope against one owning server and session.
272	- The client makes a UUID operation id per command and sends it as the wire `op`.
273	- **Logged before run.** Today `operations.log` gets a request line only for creations, and the reply line after the command ran; `serve` skips a command only when a reply line exists. That leaves a crash between sending keys and appending the reply as a repeat on retry. The port closes that gap for every non-replayable command (`Class::NonReplayable`: `session.send`, `session.resume`): `serve` appends the request line **before** dispatch, and a failed append refuses the command without running it. On arrival, an op with a request line and no reply line is answered `interrupted` and **not run again**; an op with a reply line is answered from it. `session.trust` is `Idempotent` on the wire and needs neither.
274	- The client's rule per `/ops/{op}` status:
275	  - `done`: use the reply;
276	  - `interrupted`: the host started it and the outcome is unknown; never resubmit; show the session's current state and let the user decide;
277	  - `unknown`: the host never received it (nothing was logged, and the frame answers queued requests in arrival order, so a request that had reached the frame before the status query has a line); resubmitting with the same op is safe.
278	  A timeout on a command is followed by a status query, never by a blind resend.
279	- `send` puts keys into the pane, as the app's own message box does. "Accepted" means the keys were sent. Progress is the record's state: `PromptSubmitted`, then working, then `Stop` with the new last response. A send to a pane sitting at Claude Code's folder trust question is accepted but goes nowhere until `trust` answers it; the session view carries `trust_question`, and the client shows the same "Trust this folder" button the app shows.
280	- `resume` on a not-running agent is user-initiated, so allowed, but the client confirms it ("Resume spends a turn") before sending; the host never resumes on its own.
281	- Failures name the reason: not running, not resumable, unknown record, scope missing, pairing revoked, log unavailable.
282	- **A new session (2026-10-19).** `POST projects/{id}/sessions` under `control` opens a session in the project, through the same `session.new` the CLI and Dispatch use, with the body's `op` as the key: `{op, name, kind, cwd, prompt}`, `kind` one of `claude`, `codex` or `shell` (a command or a service is not opened from a device), `cwd` the project's root when absent and otherwise a directory under it, relative or absolute, refused `bad_request` when it steps out of the root or is not a directory, so a device never opens a shell elsewhere on the disk; `prompt` is an agent's first message, on its command line as the CLI puts it, so the agent is already working when the device opens the window. The reply is the command body with `made: [{kind: "session", id}]`; `/ops/{op}` carries `made` too, so a creation whose reply was lost still names its record. `info` lists `create`. The client offers it on a host that is connected, paired under `control` and serves `create`: a plus button on the Sessions tab and "New session in this project" on a listed session, opening a sheet with the host, the project by workspace, the kind, a name (the kind's word and a count when none is typed), a directory and the first message; Start posts it, reads the project's sessions again and opens the new session's window.

284	**The draft.** An agent session's prompt on the host is its Prompt Box editor (design.md, "Prompt Box status"), one document with undo, the live utterance as a provisional span, voice commands and the AI pass. A device does not keep a prompt of its own: it reads the editor's draft and works on it, so dictation from the headset, dictation at the desk and typing on either meet in one text, and a prompt begun on one device can be finished on the other. The editor exists whether or not the session is drawn on the host, as it does for a card's microphone.
285	
286	- `GET sessions/{id}/draft` (any paired device) answers `{draft: {text, live, status, status_text, can_undo, can_redo, ai, busy}}`: the rendered text, the byte range of the utterance still being recognized or null, the editor's status (`idle`, `listening`, `finishing`, `degraded`, `error`) with its reason, whether undo and redo apply, whether the host has an `OpenAI` key for the AI pass, and whether a pass is running. Only an agent session has a draft (`no_draft` otherwise). The host emits `changed {draft, id}` for an editor whose draft moved, fingerprinted a few times a second while a subscriber is connected, and a device holding the draft re-reads it; no watch is needed, since the editor is the host's own state rather than a source the worker polls.
287	- `POST sessions/{id}/draft` (control) applies one of the editor's tools and answers with the draft as it stands: `{action: "replace", text}` sets the text whole (what the device typed; last writer wins, one person), `undo`, `redo`, `clear`, `clean_up` (the AI pass, refused `failed` when the host has no key), `delete_sentence`, `delete_paragraph`, and `{action: "send", op}`, which takes the draft's text to the pane exactly as `session.send` does, under the device's op as the key, and clears the editor when it went; a repeat of a send that went is answered from the log. A send of an empty draft is refused.
288	- `POST sessions/{id}/dictation` (control) carries `{session, events}`: the device's recognizer session, a number the device picks apart from the host's own, and its speech events in order, each `{sequence, kind, utterance, revision, text}` with `kind` one of `started`, `voice_started`, `partial`, `final`, `voice_ended`, `stopped`. The host feeds them to the editor as its own recognizer's events: `started` puts the editor's status at listening, a partial is the provisional span revised in place, a final commits the utterance at its anchor, `stopped` returns the status to idle. At most 256 events of 16 KiB each per request. The reply is the draft as it stands, so the device sees its words land without waiting for the event. The device segments speech into utterances itself (the Apple recognizer starts over after a pause and closes an utterance by re-sending its words later); the editor keeps the document. Two recognizers into one editor (the desk's and the headset's) are kept apart by their session numbers.

294	#### 4.7 Tickets
295	
296	The ticket view on a device (2026-10-17) reads Dispatch through the Switchboard port, not Dispatch's own socket, which only the Mac reaches: the port serves what the app already holds from its two-second status poll, so a device costs the runner nothing. `GET dispatch/tickets` is the core's `TicketListing` (`src/core/tickets.rs`): `connected` (a runner answered the last poll; without one the tickets are the last seen), the `projects` with a pipeline (slots, running, pending, waiting on me, the queue, the supervisor's session id), and the `tickets` by project then oldest first, never the runner's write order. Each ticket is a summary: source, state and reason, the current stage's name among the `stages`, `standing` worded exactly as the Mac's page words it (`1 waiting on you`, `plan running`, `parked: <reason>`, `held: <why>`), `waits` and `urgent` as the page colours it, `current_session` and `root_project`, and every decision with its question, options, recommendation, `multiple`, state, answer and `needs_note`. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}` adds the body (bounded at the notes cap), the attempts with the session each ran in and the pull request it is bound to, the lanes by branch, and the holds; paths stay on the Mac. The collection is one resource, `tickets` with an empty id, fingerprinted with everything else: a decision made or answered, a stage moved, or the runner coming or going is one `changed` frame, to every subscriber.
297	
298	Two commands under `control`, each the Mac's own action and so Dispatch's own call: `decide` takes `{decision, answer, note?}` (the decision's id; for a `multiple` decision the options joined by commas) and is checked against the last status before anything runs (the decision pending, every option among the decision's, a note where the option needs one), and `resume` a parked ticket. The reply is deferred until Dispatch answers the call, through the same channel the content worker answers on: `{decision}` or `{ticket}` on success, the runner's reason as `failed` or `not_found`, `dispatch_off` (503) when no runner answers. A decision already answered as asked is answered again from the record, so a device that lost the reply repeats at no cost; one answered otherwise is `answered` (409). `info` lists `tickets` among the capabilities, and a client treats a host without it as having no tickets.

# Spike 22: the remote port over std

The questions from `docs/remote-client.md` §10 that the host side can
answer without a client: can a pinned-TLS HTTP and WebSocket port run on
std threads with every request answered by the frame thread, what the
handoff costs, whether the bounds of §4.1 hold under abuse, whether
Bonjour works from Rust, what a transcript costs to parse, and whether
the content-version signals of §4.4 see the changes that defeat weaker
ones. The visionOS half (a `URLSession` pinning delegate accepting the
certificate and refusing a substitute) is not here: it needs an Xcode
project and the simulator.

Standalone crate, not built by the app. Builds into the repo's shared
`target/` like every crate under this tree.

## Crates

`rustls` 0.23 on `ring` (already in the app's tree), `rcgen` 0.14 for
the self-signed certificate, `tungstenite` 0.30 over the TLS stream
(`WebSocket::from_raw_socket` after a hand-written 101, since the
request was already read), `mdns-sd` 0.21 for Bonjour with no runtime,
`sha2` and `sha1` and `base64` for the pin and the accept key. No Tokio.
The whole thing compiled clean under the app's pedantic clippy on the
first try bar lints.

## What it does

`src/main.rs` is the server: one accept thread, one thread per
connection, TLS handshake and the first request line within 5 s, writes
within 10 s, a bounded channel of 64 to a stand-in frame thread that
sleeps `--frame-ms` and then drains at most 8 requests, bumps a
revision, and gives every WebSocket subscriber one event of
`--event-bytes` from a queue of 256; a full queue drops the subscriber
with its overflow flag set, and its writer sends `resync_required` and
closes. Two connection pools: 4 unauthenticated, 12 paired (a bearer
token moves a connection over); a further accept is dropped at once.
`src/bin/bench.rs` is a pinned client (a `ServerCertVerifier` that
checks one SHA-256 and nothing else) with four phases. `tests/versions.rs`
is the content-version experiment.

## Commands

```sh
cd spikes/22-remote-port
cargo test --release                 # the pin and request parsing; the version experiment
./measure.sh                         # the three server runs below; kills the server by pid
SWITCHBOARD_SPIKE_TRANSCRIPT=<path> cargo test --release --lib parse_timing -- --ignored --nocapture   # from the repo root
```

## Results (2026-10-12, M-series MacBook Pro, loopback)

**Handoff.** 300 `GET /api/v1/info` on one kept connection, then 50
each with a fresh TLS handshake, the client sending the next request as
soon as the reply lands:

| frame | kept connection p50 / p99 | fresh TLS p50 / p99 | frame's pass cost avg / max |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 ms | 22.0 / 24.2 ms | 21.3 / 24.2 ms | 20 µs / 184 µs |
| 100 ms (hidden window) | 107.8 / 110.2 ms | 107.4 / 110.2 ms | 28 µs / 225 µs |

WebSearch takes a `mode`. Use "standard" by default: it is the normal search, quick and cheap. Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. When you plan several searches, send them in the same turn.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

# Spike 22: the remote port over std

The questions from `docs/remote-client.md` §10 that the host side can
answer without a client: can a pinned-TLS HTTP and WebSocket port run on
std threads with every request answered by the frame thread, what the
handoff costs, whether the bounds of §4.1 hold under abuse, whether
Bonjour works from Rust, what a transcript costs to parse, and whether
the content-version signals of §4.4 see the changes that defeat weaker
ones. The visionOS half (a `URLSession` pinning delegate accepting the
certificate and refusing a substitute) is not here: it needs an Xcode
project and the simulator.

Standalone crate, not built by the app. Builds into the repo's shared
`target/` like every crate under this tree.

## Crates

`rustls` 0.23 on `ring` (already in the app's tree), `rcgen` 0.14 for
the self-signed certificate, `tungstenite` 0.30 over the TLS stream
(`WebSocket::from_raw_socket` after a hand-written 101, since the
request was already read), `mdns-sd` 0.21 for Bonjour with no runtime,
`sha2` and `sha1` and `base64` for the pin and the accept key. No Tokio.
The whole thing compiled clean under the app's pedantic clippy on the
first try bar lints.

## What it does

`src/main.rs` is the server: one accept thread, one thread per
connection, TLS handshake and the first request line within 5 s, writes
within 10 s, a bounded channel of 64 to a stand-in frame thread that
sleeps `--frame-ms` and then drains at most 8 requests, bumps a
revision, and gives every WebSocket subscriber one event of
`--event-bytes` from a queue of 256; a full queue drops the subscriber
with its overflow flag set, and its writer sends `resync_required` and
closes. Two connection pools: 4 unauthenticated, 12 paired (a bearer
token moves a connection over); a further accept is dropped at once.
`src/bin/bench.rs` is a pinned client (a `ServerCertVerifier` that

Chrome's behavior here is well documented across the results, and the sources agree on the core point.

- **Common Name is ignored:** Chrome 58 and later stopped using the Common Name for server identity. Chrome now supports only a subjectAltName (Subject Alternate Name or SAN) x.509 certificate extension of type dNSName for server identity. Some sources add that NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID is an unfortunate error code, insofar as all common names are now ignored.
- **Why it's misleading:** The error name suggests a CN problem, but the real trigger is a missing SAN. One guide notes that "the hostname you connected to is not in this certificate's SAN list." Chrome also shows a diagnostic, since Chrome now shows [missing_subjectAltName] in the details on the Certificate Error page.
- **Self-signed certs:** The change affects self-signed and internal-CA certificates most. One author reports that most single name certificates and some wildcard certificates only have a Common Name and don't have use Subject Alternative Names. A TrueNAS forum answer makes the same point about a self-signed WebGUI cert, and says you'll need to generate a certificate with the hostname/IP in that field.
- **Fix:** Regenerate the certificate with a SAN entry of type dNSName (or an IP SAN) matching the hostname or IP in the URL. For an internal CA, the fix is to reissue the cert with the SAN. Public CAs like Let's Encrypt already include it.
- **Background:** The change is based on RFC 2828 and CA/Browser Forum guidance deprecating CN-based identity. One author criticizes the change as a departure from existing practice, since other browsers still accepted CN-only certificates at the time.

Sources: RSA community article (community.rsa.com), expta blog (2017), textslashplain.com (2017), xitoring.com KB, and TrueNAS forums.

The search turned up Apple's HT210176 page (Chinese-language version) and several secondary sources that quote its requirements. I did not retrieve the English Apple page directly.

Apple's requirements for TLS server certificates in iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 that cover your question:

- **Validity period:** The certificate must last 825 days or less, measured by its NotBefore and NotAfter fields. TLS server certificates must have a validity period of 825 days or fewer (as expressed in the NotBefore and NotAfter fields of the certificate). Apple's own Chinese-language page gives the same limit, and warns that TLS server connections that violate these new requirements will fail.
- **Subject Alternative Name:** The server's DNS name must appear in the SAN extension, and the CommonName field no longer counts. Per one quoted excerpt, TLS server certificates must present the DNS name of the server in the Subject Alternative Name extension of the certificate. DNS names in the CommonName of a certificate are no longer trusted.
- **Related requirements:** The 825-day and EKU rules apply to certificates issued after July 1, 2019. Apple also requires an EKU extension containing the id-kp-serverAuth OID, and the same excerpt lists RSA keys of at least 2048 bits and SHA-2 signatures.

Sources conflict slightly on scope. The Sophos excerpts list the 2048-bit and SHA-2 rules as applying to all TLS server certificates, while the EKU and 825-day rules apply only to certificates issued after July 1, 2019. Verify against Apple's English HT210176 page before relying on this for compliance.

The search turned up mixed results. Some sources say the override works on iOS, while others say iOS Safari gives no way past a self-signed certificate.

- **Override path:** A Peplink forum user said that on iOS you tap "show details" on the error page, then "visit this website," and tested it on the latest iOS at the time. Assuming you are using Safari on your iDevices you can choose to accept the self signed certificate being presented by your router. Tap on "show details" when you get the error page, and then on "visit this website".
- **Override not working:** An Apple Community thread from January 2026 describes a NAS on iOS 26.2.1 where the "Show Details" button responds but nothing happens. The suggested fixes were to remove VPN or security add-on apps, force-restart the iPhone, and try again. The same thread suggests the certificate's hostname may be a `.local` name rather than the IP address. (I get a screen where I should be able to click on show details on iOS 26.2.1 but I can click on it but nothing happends.)
- **Strict rejection:** A Netgear Orbi community thread from November 2025 reports that on IOS, all browsers are built on Apple Webkit and so none of them will connect. The Kurento documentation says iOS Safari is the big exception to the above comment. It will outright reject untrusted self-signed certs, instead of showing a security warning.
- **Workaround:** The Kurento docs say the fix is to install the certificate's root CA on the device. The ThinLinc docs describe installing it under Settings > General > Profile, then enabling full trust in the Certificate Trust Settings. They also note that in Safari, the certificates must match the server hostname, so connecting by bare IP address can fail even with an override.

Overall, the override path seems to work for some users on some iOS versions. Other users report it failing or not appearing at all. If it doesn't work, the reliable options are to install and trust the device's root CA on iOS, or to use a hostname that matches the certificate.

Fette","url":"https://ietf.org/rfc/rfc6455"}]

The search didn't return the RFC 6455 text directly, but a GitHub discussion quotes its client-side rule, and it corrects the premise of your query.

- **The failure rule is on the client.** A GitHub comment quoting the RFC says that if the server's response names a subprotocol the client did not request, the client must fail the WebSocket connection (the server has indicated a subprotocol not requested by the client), the client MUST Fail the WebSocket Connection). Nothing in these results shows the server being required to echo a subprotocol.
- **Omitting the header is not a failure under the RFC.** A W3C bug report says RFC 6455 itself doesn't require a client to abort connection establishment when the server selects no subprotocol. The report argues that the omitted-header case should be treated as failure, and proposes clarifying the spec text.
- **Real servers have hit this.** An Asterisk issue reports that the server always answered with a subprotocol even when the client omitted one, and notes that the spec actually says the client MUST Fail the WebSocket Connection if the client omits the protocol but the server supplies one.
- **Practical advice from the same thread.** A gobwas/ws maintainer notes that a server cannot enforce a subprotocol the client did not offer. The mechanism exists so both sides agree on one, so the server should select only from the client's list, and the client should fail if the server picks something it did not offer.

I did not verify the RFC's exact wording against the primary text, so check section 4.1 and section 4.2.2 of RFC 6455 before relying on these details.

The search turned up several reports of Safari not sending SameSite=Strict cookies on WebSocket handshakes, but no single definitive fix.

- **Apple Developer Forums:** One developer saw the request not sending the previously received cookies on a second connection to the same server. The cookies were HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict. Removing HttpOnly made Safari work, and the same setup works fine on Chrome/Firefox.
- **WebKit bug 232666:** This is the closest match. Strict cookies are not sent via WebSocket on any restored/cache-loaded tabs. The report says this affected Safari 14 and 15, and it seems to be fixed on Safari 15.1. Its status is RESOLVED CONFIGURATION CHANGED.
- **WebKit bug 200345:** A 2021 comment describes the same pattern. Strict cookies were sent on XHR but not WebSocket requests. A reload did not help, but the tab can be "fixed" by focusing the location bar with the URL and pressing enter. The commenter suspects this works because the page then loads through a top-level navigation.
- **WebKit bug 298616:** This is a newer report. SignalR WebSocket handshakes fail in Safari on iOS 26 but work in Chrome and Firefox on the same device. It may not be the same cookie issue, so I wouldn't assume it is.

My takeaway: the strict-cookie problem appears tied to tabs restored or loaded from history rather than to a plain new WebSocket, and reports suggest it was fixed around Safari 15.1. I did not find a current status for the iOS 26 issue or confirm whether the older fix still holds. Verify against your Safari version before relying on this.

(WebKit Bug 41419)","url":"https://lists.webkit.org/pipermail/webkit-help/2011-May/002132.html"}]

The search turned up a few relevant sources, though none is a current, authoritative fix for this exact problem.

- **WebKit bug 41419 (open since 2010):** A developer reported that secure wss:// websocket servers could not be reached from Safari 5 or the WebKit nightly, even after the self-signed certificate was added to the keychain. Chrome worked with the same servers.
- **Mailing-list follow-up (2011):** A contributor described the behavior: after a user accepts an untrusted HTTPS certificate in iOS Safari, a wss:// connection to the same host still fails in Safari and WebKit. Chrome, by contrast, treats that acceptance as covering both protocols. The post asked whether WebKit could adopt that behavior as the fix.
- **WebKit bug 158345:** A commenter noted that the workaround is to do a normal page load first, and then do websocket requests after accepting the cert in the UI. The same comment says Chrome and Safari also rejected a self-signed certificate that lacked a Subject Alternative Name, and includes an OpenSSL command that adds one.
- **ManageEngine's Desktop Central guide:** This vendor article describes the same symptom in its HTML5 viewer. Its fix is to open the certificate prompt, choose Trust, and set it to Always Trust so Safari allows the secure WebSocket connection.

The sources suggest that Safari's per-host exception from the HTTPS warning may not carry over to wss://, and that a certificate missing a SAN can also cause failures. The WebKit bugs are old, and I didn't find a current Safari release note confirming whether this is still broken. I'd recommend testing with a SAN-bearing certificate, loading the page over HTTPS first, and checking whether the trust setting is applied to the WebSocket host.

The search didn't directly answer whether `window.isSecureContext` stays `true` after a certificate error is bypassed in Chromium. It turned up related material on the bypass itself:

- **Bypass mechanics:** In many Chromium-based browsers, this warning includes an Advanced option with a "Proceed anyway" link. One vendor article describes an undocumented keyword, "thisisunsafe," which triggers the same action as clicking Proceed anyway, even when the UI option is hidden. That source is a support article from a vendor, not Chromium documentation, so treat it with caution.
- **Visual indicator:** A Launchpad bug comparing browsers reports that Chromium displays a padlock with a cross over it, and the "https" part of the address is struck through after an exception is accepted, while Firefox shows a normal padlock.
- **Chromium source:** The Chromium devtools security handler source in the results doesn't address this behavior.
- **isSecureContext history:** A Mozilla bug thread discusses implementing `Window.isSecureContext()` as an early, basic version, but it doesn't cover certificate-error cases.

My own understanding, not confirmed by these results: `isSecureContext` is based on the origin's scheme and trustworthiness rather than on certificate validity, so an accepted-error `https` page may still report `true`. That needs verification against the Chromium source or spec before relying on it. A follow-up search on the Chromium secure-context implementation or the W3C Secure Contexts spec would be the next step.

The search didn't confirm the Firefox 58 part of your query. The results point to Firefox 48 as the version that made this change, not 58.

- **Version:** One source says this follows a similar change in Firefox 48, after Chrome's change. Another says Chrome 58 and Firefox 48 both don't accept certificates that contain only a Common Name.
- **Behavior:** Newer browsers look for a hostname or IP in the SAN extension rather than the CN. One RSA note says New versions of Chrome (Chrome 58) and Firefox check the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field, looking for a DNS name or IP address.
- **Mixed reports:** One bug report says that on my machine (NixOS, Firefox 62) it still works, others say it doesn't work. A Squid mailing list reply describes the Chrome-specific message and says this is not a problem with Firefox, which conflicts with the Firefox 48 claim.

- **Fix:** The common advice is to regenerate the certificate with a SAN entry matching the hostname or IP. One forum post describes adding SAN settings to the OpenSSL config and notes that certificates generated by Let's Encrypt do this automatically.

A follow-up search for Firefox's own release notes or bug tracker entry would be the best way to confirm the exact version and error string.

The search found the per-host connection limit for iOS Safari but no published keep-alive idle timeout for it.

- **Connection limit:** A Diffusion vendor guide lists iOS Safari at 6 connections, and says that the maximum number of connections is per browser and not per browser tab. This is a secondary source and may not reflect current iOS versions. A table from around Safari 7.0.1 also lists 6 connections per hostname.
- **Origin of the limit:** The same guide says the figure comes from an old spec. The HTTP 1.1 protocol states that single-user clients should not maintain more than two connections with any server or proxy. Browsers have exceeded that recommendation.
- **Keep-alive timeout:** MDN describes the `Keep-Alive: timeout` parameter as an integer that is the time in seconds that the host will allow an idle connection to remain open before it is closed. It is a server hint, and a host may keep an idle connection open for longer than timeout seconds. I found no Safari-specific idle timeout value.
- **HTTP/2 caveat:** Connection-specific header fields such as Connection and Keep-Alive are prohibited in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Safari does not load any response that contains them. The six-connection cap matters mainly for HTTP/1.1.
- **Native apps, not Safari:** An Apple developer forum thread notes that httpMaximumConnectionsPerHost is expected to control the number of simultaneous connections to a host, not the number of simultaneous requests. This applies to URLSession, not Safari.

Bottom line: iOS Safari is commonly cited at 6 connections per host for HTTP/1.1. The keep-alive idle timeout is server-defined, and I found no documented iOS Safari value. Verifying would need Apple's WebKit source or a direct test.

# Issue #230 facts (browser page on the remote port)

Searches were run with WebSearch (standard mode) and fetched with WebFetch; the exact queries are under each claim. Where a query returned nothing usable the claim is marked Unresolved. No spike was run: every question a browser would answer needs a browser or a device, and none can be run here. The spec and RFC questions were settled by reading the text.

## Settled

1. Chrome 58 and later ignore the subject Common Name and take server identity only from subjectAltName dNSName entries; a certificate with only a CN gives NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID.
   - https://textslashplain.com/2017/03/10/chrome-deprecates-subject-cn-matching/ ("certificates specify the hostname(s) ... in the SubjectAltName field"; "values in the Subject field will be ignored")
   - https://community.rsa.com/s/article/Google-Chrome-reports-NET-ERR-CERT-COMMON-NAME-INVALID-due-to-missing-Subject-Alternative-Names-when-accessing-the-RSA-Identity-Router-Single-Sign-On-Portal (vendor KB: missing SAN causes the error)
   - Query: "Chrome ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID self-signed certificate without subjectAltName Common Name ignored"
   - Covers: Chrome 58 onward. Two sources agree.

2. Apple states these requirements for TLS server certificates (iOS 13 and macOS 10.15): the DNS name in subjectAltName; validity of 825 days or fewer (for certificates issued after 1 July 2019); an EKU with id-kp-serverAuth; RSA keys of at least 2048 bits; SHA-2 signatures. The page says "Connections to TLS servers violating these new requirements will fail."
   - https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT210176 (fetched; verbatim quotes)
   - Query: "Apple HT210176 requirements for TLS server certificates subject alternative name 825 days iOS 13"
   - The page does not say whether these bind a certificate the user trusts by hand. See Unresolved 1.
   - The tree's identity fails all of them: `src/adapters/remote.rs:102-110` sets no SAN, no EKU, and the default validity, and the notes say `not_after` is in the year 4096.

3. A WebSocket client must fail the connection if the server names a subprotocol the client did not offer. If the server sends no Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header, the RFC does not make that a failure. The server must send none unless it selects a value from the client's list, and the value is a token.
   - https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455 §4.1 item 6 and §4.2.2 (fetched; verbatim)
